rows.verified: HSE warehousing guidance applies to employers, employees and people working around warehouses, including hauliers and couriers.
Storage and warehousing risk management should address the main causes of injury and ill health in the sector.
Manual handling and being struck by moving vehicles are prominent warehouse hazards.
Warehouse controls should cover mechanical handling, workplace transport, work at height and accident or emergency arrangements.
Storage racking and other equipment should display safe-working-load information where safe use depends on avoiding overload.
Steel and metal-stock storage requires controls for loading, unloading, lifting, sharp edges and stable storage systems.
Warehouse major-accident assessment should consider failure modes including fire, explosion, impact, overheating and structural failure.
Inspection, safe plant layout, isolation, emergency response and containment can form part of warehouse risk control.
Warehouse risk depends on stock type, racking design, loading, traffic routes, handling methods, worker competence, maintenance and emergency planning.
HSE warehouse evidence is site-, stock-, racking-, vehicle-, worker- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
Powered gates are machines that must be designed, manufactured, installed and maintained to prevent serious or fatal injury.
Powered-gate hazards include impact, crushing, trapping, access to moving mechanisms and electric, hydraulic or pneumatic risks.
Outdoor weather, wind, debris and water ingress can affect gate stability, electrical safety and reliable operation.
Gate design must account for location, vulnerable users, foreseeable misuse, normal wear and environmental conditions.
Safety can require a combination of hazard elimination, guarding, speed control, force limitation, pressure-sensitive edges and suitable sensors.
Powered gates require continuing maintenance, inspection, testing and adjustment because components can wear or fail.
A powered gate found to be dangerous should be taken out of use until the safety concerns are adequately addressed.
Users should receive operating, maintenance and emergency-release information, and competent people should perform installation and safety work.
Powered-gate risk depends on geometry, force, speed, sensors, foundations, weather, maintenance, users and emergency-release arrangements.
HSE powered-gate evidence is product-, installation-, location-, user-, maintenance- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
